title: U.K. funder uses ‘AI triage’ to reject grant proposals—leaving researchers dismayed
key_facts: The CRANE phase one pilot, a cybersecurity funding call hosted at the University of Oxford and funded by the Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council (part of UK Research and Innovation, UKRI), used 'AI-based review' as an initial triage of 179 proposals.

Several AI models scored proposals against seven criteria (including relevance, quality and novelty, feasibility, value for money); a second pass with different models was run and scores combined; only the top half went to human review.

Rejected applicants include Lancaster University academics John Stott (astrophysics) and Claire Hardaker (forensic linguistics), whose rejected bid was partly about misplaced confidence in fluent-sounding AI.
The call document had warned applicants that AI tools might be used in initial assessment, with final decisions by the award panel.

A UKRI spokesperson said UKRI policy does not allow generative AI to conduct application assessment and that it is following up with the CRANE network to review compliance; UKRI told THE that releasing confidential material into generative AI tools breaches its confidentiality and integrity policies.

UKRI has separately proposed measures against the AI-driven surge in applications, including in-person interviews for higher-risk awards and 'exploring the safe use of AI-assisted assessment' with safeguards.
THE reported the story on 27 Sep 2026; Research Professional News followed on 28 Sep 2026 (funder defends data security); Science published its account on 3-4 Oct 2026.
quote_evidence: Academics have expressed dismay after artificial intelligence was used to reject half of the grant proposals in a UK Research and Innovation-funded call.

why_it_matters_hint: A UKRI-funded network screened out half of 179 grant bids with AI before any human read them, which UKRI says its own policy forbids.
